summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful in Montserrat since 2001. The reform was made retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000, and formed part of a single British decision to scrap anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, on the stated ground that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The order was imposed from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent.

Residual criminal exposure remains and turns on the sex of the partners and the setting. Lesbian activity was never an offence in Montserrat. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone. The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so conduct lawful between opposite-sex partners of the same age can be an offence between same-sex partners.

As a British Overseas Territory, Montserrat stands under the United Kingdom's framework and must comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations. Domestically, Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with 'discriminatory' defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

A visitor should expect almost no visible organised LGBT social infrastructure. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.
tangentialFactors:
Local social life is scarce for reasons with physical causes as much as legal ones. Hurricane Hugo in 1989 and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption wastelanded the south of the 104 km2 island and displaced more than half the population northward; reporting from 2012 describes the gay scene as decimated and quotes the observation that gay people 'are everywhere but hardly here'.

The 2001 reform was not a local initiative. Reporting from January 2001 frames the decriminalisation of Montserrat and four other Caribbean territories as a cultural rift with London, with local politicians and religious leaders opposing a decision taken and transmitted from the United Kingdom.
localsOnly:
Article 79 of the Labour Code's prohibition on discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation operates for people working and resident in Montserrat, alongside the constitutional guarantee in Article 16.

The constitutional and statutory protections are stated in terms of sexual orientation generally rather than gender identity, so their application to a resident's everyday employment or service disputes rests on how 'discriminatory' is read across the listed grounds, which include sex and other status.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific legal material for Montserrat: recognition or change of gender markers on passports or local identity documents, any medical or psychological screening requirement, and access to gender-affirming care are unsourced here and should be verified against current United Kingdom and Montserrat instruments before reliance.

No enforcement data is sourced for the residual offences of group sex and sex in public, nor for any reported incident of anti-LGBT violence, its date, or its outcome. The identity of the hotels operating non-discrimination policies is not given in the sources reviewed.

The age-of-consent differential is stated in the sources without a worked enforcement example, and no source addresses how it has been applied.
